coredata.dc:description: The substrate specificities of three extracellular polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) depolymerases from Alcaligenes faecalis (PhaZAfa), Pseudomonas stutzeri (PhaZPst), and Comamonas acidovorans (PhaZCac), which are grouped into types A and B based on the position of a lipase box sequence in the catalytic domain, were examined for films of 12 different aliphatic polyesters. Each of these PHB depolymerases used was capable of hydrolyzing poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (P(3HB)), poly(3-hydroxypropionate) (P(3HP)), poly(4-hydroxybutyrate) (P(4HB)), poly(ethylene succinate) (PESU), and poly(ethylene adipate) (PEA) but could not hydrolyze another seven polyesters. In addition, the binding characteristics of substrate binding domains from PhaZAfa, PhaZCac, and PHB depolymerase from Comamonas testosteroni (PhaZCte) were studied by using fusions with glutathione S-transferase (GST). All of fusion proteins adsorbed strongly on the surfaces of polyester granules of P(3HB), P(3HP), and poly(2-hydroxypropionate) (P(2HP)) which was not hydrolyzed by the PHB depolymerases used in this study, while they did not bind on Avicel and chitin granules. The adsorption kinetics of the fusion proteins to the surface of P(3HB) and P(2HP) granules were found to obey the Langmuir isotherm. The cross-area per molecule of fusion protein bound to P(3HB) granules was estimated to be 12±4 nm2/molecule. It has been suggested that the active sites in catalytic domains of PHB depolymerases have a similar conformational structure, and that several amino acids in substrate-binding domains of PHB depolymerases interact specifically with the surface of polyesters.

ce:section.ce:para: A wide variety of bacteria synthesize an optically active polymer of (R)-3-hydroxybutyric acid and accumulate it as a reserve energy source [1,2]. Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate) (P(3HB)) isolated from bacteria is a partially crystalline polymer with a melting temperature around 180°C [3]. A remarkable characteristic of P(3HB) is its biodegradability in various environments. Aerobic and anaerobic P(3HB)-degrading microorganisms have been isolated from many ecosystems[4,5], and the properties of their extracellular polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) depolymerases have been studied [6–12]. Analysis of the genes revealed that the enzymes have bifunctional organization composed of two domains and a linker region [6,13]. One of the domains plays the role in binding to solid P(3HB) and is called a substrate-binding domain (SBD) [14–17]. The other domain is a catalytic domain and contains catalytic machinery composed of a catalytic triad (Ser-His-Asp) [18,19]. The serine is a part of a lipase box pentapeptide Gly-X-Ser-X-Gly [20], which has been found in all known serine hydrolases, such as lipases, esterases, and serine proteases [21–23]. In addition, the two domains are connected by a fibronectin type III or threonin-rich linker [19,24,25].

In a previous study [26], the kinetics of adsorption and hydrolysis using a PHB depolymerase from Alcaligenes faecalis T1 were investigated on the surface of five polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) films. It was found that the enzyme was adsorbed on the surface of all five PHA films, but the enzyme hydrolyzed only three PHA films (P(3HB), P(3HP), and P(4HB)) and did not hydrolyze other two PHA films of P(2HP) and poly(6-hydroxyhexanoate). In addition, our previous works [16,17,27] using fusion proteins of a SBD of PHB depolymerase with glutathione S-transferase have demonstrated that the SBD moiety is essential for the adsorption of PHB depolymerase to the surface of P(3HB) granules and acts independently of the catalytic domain.

The primary structures of PHB depolymerases reported are classified into two groups based on the location of a lipase box sequence in the catalytic domains (Fig. 1 ). In type A PHB depolymerases a lipase box is located in the center of catalytic domain, while a lipase box is adjacent to N termini in type B PHB depolymerases. However, there are few reports on the relationship between the primary structure of PHB depolymerase and kinetic behavior of enzymatic hydrolysis.

The objective of the present study is to understand the mechanism of enzymatic hydrolysis for polyesters by PHB depolymerases. This paper reports the substrate and binding specificities of four PHB depolymerases from A. faecalis, Pseudomonas stutzeri, Comamonas acidovorans, and Comamonas testosteroni, defined as types A and B.

The molecular weights, thermal properties and crystallinities of 12 polyester samples used in this study are listed in Table 1 . P(3HB) was purchased from Polyscience Inc. Poly(3-hydroxypentanoate) ((P(3HV)) was produced by a recombinant Ralstonia eutropha from pentanoic acid [28]. Poly(3-hydroxyoctanoate) ((P(3HO)) was produced by Pseudomonas oleovorans ATCC 29347 from octanoic acid [29]. Poly(4-hydroxybutyrate) ((P(4HB)) was produced by C. acidovorans IFO 13582 from 1,4-butanediol [30]. Poly(3-hydroxypropionate) ((P(3HP)), poly(5-hydroxypentanoate) (P(5HV)), and poly(6-hydroxyhexanoate) (P(6HH) were prepared at 60°C by ring-opening polymerizations of β-propiolactone, δ-valelolactone, and ε-caprolactone in the presence of poly(methylaluminoxane) catalyst, respectively [31]. Poly(2-hydroxypropionate) (P(2HP)) was purchased from Shimadzu Inc. Poly(ethylene adipate) (PEA), poly(ethylene succinate) (PESU), poly(butylene adipate) (PBA), and poly(butylene succinate) (PBSU) were kind gifts of Showa High Polymer Inc. Polyester films were prepared by solvent-casting techniques from chloroform solution of polyester using glass Petri dishes as casting surface [32]. Avicel and chitin were purchased from Asahi and Sigma, respectively.

Escherichia coli DH5α[supE44, ΔlacU169(φ80 lacZΔM15), hsdR17, recA1, endA1, gyrA96, thi1, relA1] (Toyobo, Osaka, Japan) was used as host for the production of recombinant proteins. A. faecalis T1 (=JCM 10169) [33], P. stutzeri YM1006 (=JCM 10168) [34], and C. acidovorans YM1609 (=JCM 10172) [16,35] were used as sources for PHB depolymerases. Recombinant R. eutropha [28], C. acidovorans IFO 13582, and P. oleovorans ATCC 29347 were used for the production of P(3HV), P(4HB), and (P(3HO), respectively. Plasmids pGEX-SBDAfa [27], pGEX-SBDCte [17], and pGEX-SBDCac [16] encoding substrate-binding domains (SBDs) of depolymerases from A. faecalis JCM 10169, C. testosteroni YM1004 (=JCM 10170) [36], and C. acidovorans JCM 10172 were used as expression vectors for glutathione S-transferase (GST)-SBD fusion proteins. The four P(3HB)-degrading bacterium strains used in this study were deposited in the Japan Collection of Microorganisms (JCM), Saitama, Japan.

A. faecalis JCM 10169, P. stutzeri JCM 10168, and C. acidovorans JCM 10172 were grown at 30°C in a mineral salt medium containing 0.46% KH2PO4, 1.16% Na2HPO4·12H2O, 0.15% P(3HB) granules, 0.05% MgSO4·7H2O, 0.01% FeCl3·6H2O, 0.005% CaCl2·2H2O, and 0.1% NH4Cl. The mineral agar plates were prepared by addition of 1.5% agar to the above liquid culture. E. coli cells harboring plasmids were grown in Luria–Bertani broth or M9 medium containing 0.01% ampicillin at 37°C.

The PHB depolymerases from A. faecalis (PhaZAfa), P. stutzeri (PhaZPst), and C. acidovorans (PhaZCac) were purified to electrophoretic homogeneity by the methods described previously [16,34,37]. The enzymatic hydrolysis of polyester films by the purified PHB depolymerases were carried out at 37°C in 0.1 M potassium phosphate buffer (pH 7.4). The polyester films (initial weights: 14 mg, initial film dimension: 10×10×0.1 mm) were placed in small bottles containing 1.0 ml of the buffer. The reaction was started by the addition of an aqueous solution of PHB depolymerase (PhaZAfa: 1 μg, PhaZPst: 4 μg, PhaZCac: 2 μg). For the weight loss measurement, the reaction solution was incubated for 5 h at 37±0.1°C with shaking, and the sample films were removed after the reaction, washed with distilled water, and dried to constant weight in vacuo before analysis.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Construction and expression of a GST–SBD fusion proteins
ce:section.ce:para: The construction of recombinant plasmids were carried out using pGEX 4T-1 vector as reported previously [16,17,27]. The resulting plasmid pGEX-SBD expressed a GST–SBD fusion protein that includes a SBD of PHB depolymerase in E. coli DH 5α (Fig. 1). Purifications of the GST–SBD fusion proteins from the supernatant were performed using Bulk GST purification module (Pharmacia, Uppsala, Sweden) according to the manufacture’s instructions.

P(3HB), P(2HP), P(3HP), chitin, and Avicel granules were used as the adsorbents. P(3HB) granules were purified by washing with distilled water, acetone, and hexane. P(3HP) and P(2HP) granules were prepared and purified as follows. The polymers were dissolved in chloroform and precipitated as granules by addition of methanol. The granules were dried in vacuo at room temperature. Chitin and Avicel granules were purified by washing with distilled water. P(3HB), P(2HP), chitin, or Avicel granules (400 μg) or 10 mg of P(3HP) granules were suspended in 1.0 ml of 0.05 mM Tris–HCl buffer at pH 7.5 and preincubated at 37°C for 5 min. After preincubation, a solution of a given amount of fusion protein solution was added. The reaction mixture was incubated at 37°C for 1–60 min and then centrifuged in a Eppendorf F 45-30-11 rotor at 10 000×g for 1 min. The amount of protein in the supernatant was determined by the Bradford method [38], using bovine serum albumin as the standard. The amount of enzyme bound to polymer granules was calculated from the values of soluble and added enzyme.

The diameters of P(3HB) granules were determined by a scanning electron microscope (JEOL JSM5300) after gold coating of granules using an ion sputtering device (JEOL JFC-1100E). Scanning electron micrographs demonstrated that P(3HB) granules used in this study were smooth spheres with a uniform size distribution and that an average diameter granules was approximately 1.0 μm. Based on the measurement, it was calculated that the surface area per 1 g of P(3HB) granules was 4.9±0.5 m2.

All molecular weight data of polyesters were obtained by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) at 40°C, using a Shimadzu 6A GPC system and a 6A refractive index detector with Shodex K-80M and K-802 columns [32]. Chloroform was used as eluent at a flow rate of 0.8 ml/min, and sample concentrations of 1.0 mg/ml were applied. Polystyrene standards with a low polydispersity were used to make a calibration curve. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) data of polyesters were recorded in the temperature range −150–+200°C on a Shimadzu DSC-50 equipped with a cooling accessory under a nitrogen flow of 30 ml/min. Samples of 10 mg were encapsulated in aluminum pans and heated from 0 to 200°C at a rate of 10°C/min. The melting temperature (T m) was determined from the DSC endotherms. For measurement of the glass-transition temperature (T g), the samples were maintained at 200°C for 1 min and then rapidly quenched at −150°C. They were heated from −150 to +200°C at a heating rate of 20°C/min. The T g was taken as the midpoint of the heating capacity change. The X-ray diffraction patterns of films were recorded at 27°C on a Rigaku RAD-IIIB system using nickel-filtered Cu Kα radiation (λ=0.154 nm; 40 kV; 30 mA) in the 2θ range 6–40° at a scan speed of 2.0°/min. Degrees of crystallinity of polyester films were calculated from diffracted intensity data (Eq. (1)).

The nucleotide sequences of C. acidovorans, C. testosteroni, P. stutzeri, and A. faecalis PHB depolymerase genes are available from GenBank under the accession number AB003186, AB000508, AB012225, and J04223, respectively.

The substrate specificities of three bacterial PHB depolymerases (PhaZAfa, PhaZPst, and PhaZCac) belonging to both types A and B were investigated for 12 polyester films (Table 1). The enzymatic hydrolysis of polyester film was carried out at 37°C for 5 h in an aqueous solution. Fig. 2 shows the rates of enzymatic hydrolysis (erosion) for polyester films by three PHB depolymerases. Regardless of the difference in primary structures of catalytic domains, the PHB depolymerases hydrolyzed P(3HB), P(3HP), P(4HB), PEA, and PESU films. In contrast, none of the PHB depolymerases were able to hydrolyze any of the other polyesters. The rates of enzymatic hydrolysis for five polyester films were dependent on the kind of PHB depolymerases. The rate of enzymatic hydrolysis by PhaZAfa (Type A) decreased in the following order: P(4HB)>P(3HP)>P(3HB)>PEA>PESU, while the rate by PhaZPst (Type A) decreased as: P(3HP)>P(3HB)>PESU>P(4HB)>PEA. The rate of enzymatic hydrolysis with PhaZCac (Type B) decreased as: P(3HP)>P(4HB)>PEA>P(3HB)>PESU.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Adsorption of GST-SBD fusion proteins to polymer granules
ce:section.ce:para: Adsorption tests of GST-SBDCac, GST-SBDCte, and GST-SBDAfa were first studied at 37°C using P(3HB) granules. The amount of fusion proteins bound to P(3HB) granules increased with time and reached a constant value within 5 min (data not shown). In all experiments, the amount of fusion proteins adsorbed on the surface of polymer granules (E ad) and the concentration of fusion proteins in an aqueous solution at an adsorption equilibrium ([E]e) were determined after the mixture of fusion proteins and polymer granules was incubated for 10 min at 37°C.

The fusion proteins adsorbed to P(3HB) and P(3HP) granules (Table 2 ) and the adsorbed proteins were not released by washing with 10 mM Tris–HCl buffer or MilliQ water (data not shown), indicating that fusion proteins are strongly bound on the surface of P(3HB) and P(3HP) granules. In addition, it is noted that all fusion proteins are also bound to P(2HP) granules, a substrate which was not hydrolyzed by the PHB depolymerases. On the other hand, none of the fusion proteins was able to adsorb to Avicel or chitin granules. It was confirmed that the GST as a component of fusion protein was not bound to polyester and polysaccharide granules used in this study. These results suggest that the substrate-binding domain (SBD) of PHB depolymerase is responsible for binding on the surface of polyester granules.

Here, we performed the kinetic study on the adsorption of the fusion proteins on the surface of polyester granules of P(3HB) and P(2HP). Fig. 3 shows the relation between the amount of adsorbed protein (E ad) and the equilibrium concentration of protein ([E]e) in the presence of GST-SBDCac at 37°C. Thus, the adsorption of GST-SBDCac on the surface of polyester granules could be expressed by the Langmuir adsorption Eq. (1).

where E max and K are a maximum amount of protein adsorbed on polyester granules and the adsorption equilibrium constant of protein, respectively, and [E] is the concentration of the protein added. In addition, the adsorption kinetics of GST-SBDCte and GST-SBDAfa were also studied at 37°C for P(3HB) granules. The values of K and E max are given in Table 3 .

On the basis of the values of E max, we can calculate a cross-area per one molecule of fusion proteins bound to the surface of P(3HB) granules. The apparent cross-area per one molecule of fusion proteins on the surface of P(3HB) granule was calculated as 12±5 nm2, by using the molecular masses of fusion proteins and the surface area (4.9±0.5 m2/g) of P(3HB) granules.

In this study, to understand the relationship between structures and functions of both catalytic and substrate-binding domains we investigated the substrate and binding specificities of PHB depolymerases. Though the rates of hydrolysis were different among three PHB depolymerases, they were capable of hydrolyzing the same kinds of polyester films. The enzymatically degradable five polyesters have some common chemical structures: the number of carbon and oxygen atoms between two carbonyl groups of the backbone is 3 or 4, while the side chain is methyl carbon or hydrogen. Thus, PHB depolymerases showed relatively narrow substrate specificities for the hydrolysis of polyesters. These results suggest that the active sites of three PHB depolymerases have a similar conformational structure, independently of a difference in the sequence structure of catalytic domains.

Three fusion proteins (GST-SBDAfa, GST-SBDCac, and GST-SBDCte) did not adsorb on the polysaccharide granules of Avicel and chitin, while those were strongly bound to the surface of different polyester granules, of P(3HP), P(3HB), and P(2HP), suggesting that there are some specific interactions based on a molecular recognition between SBD and the surface of polyesters. Here, all fusion proteins are noted to be bound to P(2HP) which was not hydrolyzed by the PHB depolymerases, indicating that the binding of SBD to a substrate is necessary but not a sufficient condition for the degradation. This suggests that the binding specificity of SBD is broad compared with the substrate specificity of catalytic domain. The values of adsorption equilibrium constant K to P(3HB) granules were almost identical among three fusion proteins, indicating that the affinities between SBD and the surface of polyesters are similar to one another.

In contrast to the sequences of catalytic domains, there is significant homology between the SBDs of PHB depolymerases (Fig. 4 ). In particular four amino acid residues (histidine (H), alanine (A), arginine (R), and cysteine (C)) are completely conserved in all SBDs reported so far. In addition, six amino acid residues of tyrosine (Y) and phenylalanine (F) with an aromatic side chain and 12 residues of serine (S), threonine (T), glutamine (Q), and asparagine (N) with a polar side chain are conserved in SBDs at a comparatively high level. This suggests that some of these common amino acid residues are involved in molecular recognition between the SBDs and the surface of polyesters. In particular, positively charged histidine and arginine residues of four completely conserved residues among SBDs seem to interact with carbonyl groups of polyesters specifically and electrostatically.

The adsorption of fusion protein (GST-SBD) could be expressed by the Langmuir adsorption Eq. (1). The values of E max for three fusion proteins were in the range 25±9 (μg/mg P(3HB) granules), which suggests that the apparent cross-area per one molecule of fusion protein bound to the surface of P(3HB) granules is 12±5 nm2. The hydrodynamic radius of a fusion protein (GST-SBD) of 31 kDa molecular mass is estimated at approximately 2–3 nm on the assumption that the protein is globular [39]. The result suggests that fusion proteins adsorb densely as monolayers on the surface of P(3HB) granule under conditions of high concentrations of fusion protein.

In previous papers [40,41], we studied the kinetics and mechanism of surface hydrolysis of P(3HB) film using the PHB depolymerase from A. faecalis, and reported that the rate (R) of enzymatic hydrolysis of P(3HB) film was expressed by Eq. (2).

where k s is the rate constant of surface hydrolysis of P(3HB) chains by enzyme; K a is an apparent adsorption equilibrium constant of enzyme; and [E] is the concentration of the enzyme added. The values of k s and K a at 37°C were determined as 8.3±1.0 (μmol/h) and 0.6±0.2 (ml/μg), respectively, with the PHB depolymerase from A. faecalis [41]. As presented in Eq. (2), the rate of enzymatic hydrolysis of P(3HB) surface increases to a maximum value with the concentration of PHB depolymerase, followed by a gradual decrease. The kinetic behavior has been accounted for in terms of a surface–enzymatic reaction that the hydrolysis of P(3HB) chains takes place by the surface reaction between adsorbed enzymes and free adsorption points on the surface [41]. Then, the rate (R) is expressed by Eq. (3).
(3) R=ksθ(1−θ)
The ratio of surface–occupation (θ) of enzyme molecules is given by the Langmuir adsorption (Eq. (1)). Here it is noted that the K value (0.8±0.1 ml/μg) of GST-SBDAfa is almost consistent with the K a value (0.6±0.2 ml/μg) of A. faecalis PHB depolymerase at 37°C.

At high concentrations larger than 2 μg/ml of PHB depolymerase, the rate of enzymatic hydrolysis on P(3HB) surface decreases with the concentration of enzyme [40,41], which is accounted for in terms of a self-blocking inhibition owing to a condense adsorption of a dual functional PHB depolymerase consisting of catalytic and substrate-binding domains. The two domains may be connected by a flexible linker protein and function independently. It may be concluded that at low concentrations below 1 μg/ml of PHB depolymerase the majority of catalytic domains of adsorbed enzymes are able to hydrolyze P(3HB) chains on the surface, while that at high concentrations of the enzyme the majority of catalytic domains are not accessible to P(3HB) chains due to a condense coverage of the substrate-binding domains on the surface of P(3HB).
